Judgment:

(Per the Hon'ble Sri Justice P.SAM KOSHY) The instant is an appeal under Section 374(2) of the Cr.P.C filed by the appellant - accused challenging the judgment of conviction dated 21.02.2014 in S.C.No.748 of 2012 passed by the III Additional District and Sessions Judge, Ranga Reddy District.

entities.text: Additional District and Sessions Judge, Ranga Reddy District
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. Heard Mr. P. Bhanu Prakash, learned counsel for the appellant and the learned Public Prosecutor appearing for the respondent - State.

3. Vide the impugned judgment, the appellant has been found guilty of having committed the offence under Section 302 of IPC, 1860 (for short, 'IPC') and has been sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life with fine of Rs.1,000/- and in default to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of three (03) months.
4. As could be seen from the impugned judgment, the appellant herein is the husband of Mohd.
Parveen Begum (hereinafter, the 'deceased')

and they are residents of Indira Gandhi Puram,
Fathenagar, Hyderabad.
The prosecution has alleged that the husband of the deceased, who is addicted to alcohol, continued to doubt her loyalty and harassed the deceased both mentally and physically in a drunken condition.
On 26.04.2012, at around 22:00 hours, under the influence of alcohol, he argued with his wife and in a fit of rage, doused her with kerosene and set her on fire.
5. PWs.1 to 6 who heard the hues and cries of the deceased went to the rescue the deceased and made their attempts to gain entry by knocking.
The accused, who was inside, did not open the door.

The local residents broke the door and found the deceased engulfed in flames, quickly doused her with water, wrapped her in a blanket to extinguish the flames and rushed her to Gandhi Hospital in an ambulance for better treatment.
Based on the information received, the Inspector of Police assigned ASI M. Manikappa (PW.11) to record the statement of the injured party.

Subsequently,
PW.11 visited the hospital and recorded the dying declaration of the deceased and on the basis of the said statement; PW.11 registered a case against the accused in Crime No.234 of 2012 under Section 498A of IPC.
Further PW.11 also filed a requisition before the X Addl. CMM at Hyderabad on 27.04.2012 at 3:50 hrs.

However, the statement of the woman who suffered burn injuries could not Md. Rafeeq, Hyd., vs State Of Telangana, Rep. Pp., on 11 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/154949575/
1 be recorded because she was unconscious when the X Addl. CMM visited the hospital.

sentences.text:
Subsequently,
upon the request of the police, the Deputy Collector carried out an inquest on the body of the deceased.
On 27.04.2012, the police apprehended the appellant and remanded him to Court.
After concluding their investigation, the police submitted a charge- sheet for this case.
On 08.5.2012, a second request was made to the Hon'ble IX ACMM to record the dying declaration of the woman who had been burnt.
PW.12 (P. Rajasekhar, Hon'ble IX ACCM Court) visited Gandhi Hospital in Secunderabad on the same day at 17.30 hrs and recorded the woman's dying declaration.
On 09.05.2012, the deceased died in the hospital while undergoing treatment.
Then the police altered the Section of law from 498A and 307 of IPC to Sections 498A and 302 of IPC and submitted a memo to that extent.
6. Further the learned IX Metropolitan Magistrate, Cyberabad at Kukatpally took cognizance of the case against the appellant for the offence under Sections 498A and 302 of IPC.

As the case is within the jurisdiction of Sessions, it was committed to the court of Sessions, Metropolitan Sessions Judge,
Cyberabad after adopting the procedure as laid down under Section 209 Cr.P.C., who registered a case against the appellant as S.C.No.748 of 2012 for the offence under Sections 498A and 302 of IPC and made over to the Court below for trial and disposal in accordance to law.
To prove the charges under Section 302 of IPC, the prosecution in all examined fifteen (15) witnesses and marked Exs.P1 to P10.
No witnesses were examined in defence.
The Trail Court after recording the statement of the appellant under Section 313 of Cr.P.C finally passed the impugned judgment of conviction which is under challenge in the instant appeal.
7. The present appeal has been filed on the ground that the Trail court has failed to appreciate the fact that the evidence of PWs.1 to 4 is unnatural and unbelievable.
There is no eye witness to the incident except the statement of the deceased and the evidence of the PWs is not corroborating with each other and there are discrepancies in their evidence.

The Trail Court based on Exs.P4 and P6 i.e.
dying declaration recorded by the Police and Magistrate which are not recorded as per procedure was not justified in convicting the appellant.

8. The facts of the case in brief are that the deceased who is the wife of the appellant (Mohd. Rafeeq)
was in love with him seven (07) years back and with consent of the elders they both got married and one daughter was born out of their wedlock.
The appellant had abandoned his wife and daughter for several years and during that time the deceased had to work as a labourer to support herself and her daughter.
However, three months before the incident, the appellant returned to the deceased and assured the deceased that he would take proper care of her and the daughter.
Trusting her husband's promise, the deceased allowed him to live with her.
Unfortunately, her hopes were short-lived as her husband, who is addicted to alcohol, continued to doubt her loyalty and harassed her again.
On 26.04.2012, at around 22:00 hours, under the influence of alcohol, he argued with his wife and in a fit of rage, doused her with kerosene and set her on fire.
As a result, she sustained severe burn injuries.
Their neighbours intervened by extinguishing the flames and covering the woman's burnt body with clothes.
Subsequently, she was admitted in women burns ward Gandhi Hospital, Secunderabad.

2 9.

entities.text: Md. Rafeeq, Hyd., vs State Of Telangana, Rep. Pp
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that there are discrepancies in the evidences of PWs.1 to 4 and has no corroboration to each other.

There are two dying declarations, out of them,
one is recorded by PW.11 while the other is recorded by PW.12 and there are contradictions between these two statements.
Therefore, the Trail Court could not have relied on the alleged dying declarations.
The learned counsel for the appellant tried to argue that the deceased might have committed suicide but the case was projected as if it was a murder said to have been committed by the appellant.
There is no evidence to accept that the appellant himself committed the offence of murder, thereby, sought for acquittal of the appellant.

10. Opposing the appeal, the learned Public Prosecutor referring to the deposition of PW.12 who has taken the dying declaration contended that the case of the prosecution stands established from the dying declaration which has been subsequently proved from the statement of the Magistrate who recorded the same.
Therefore, the impugned judgment does not warrant interference.

11. Similarly, the learned Public Prosecutor also referred to the deposition of PWs.2 and 3, the two persons who had reached the scene of occurrence immediately after the incident had occurred and both of whom have also supported the case of the prosecution so far as reaching the scene of occurrence first contributing in extinguishing the fire on the body of the deceased, wrapping up in a blanket and thereafter making arrangements for taking the deceased to hospital to save her life.
Referring to all these evidences, the learned Public Prosecutor also contended that the reaction of the husband in not taking steps to extinguish the fire also goes against the appellant.

12. With all the aforesaid submissions, the learned Public Prosecutor contended that the case of the prosecution stands established beyond all reasonable doubts and hence the appeal deserves to be dismissed.

13. Having heard the contentions put forth on either side an on perusal of records, it would be relevant at this juncture, to take note of the statement recorded by the PW.11 whereby the deceased stated as under:
"Today i.e., on 26.04.2012 in the night at about 10:00pm my husband came in a drunken condition and picked up quarrel with me and also beat me.
When I said to him that I will die, he replied me to die, he poured kerosene on me and I set ablaze myself.
My whole body was burnt."

14. In contrast to the above statement, the deceased gave her dying declaration to PW.12 on 08.05.2012 as under:
"ye sab sola din kebaadhogay.
Hamaraaadmi Md Rafi ham ko kerosene daalkar jaladiye.
Use time me hum aur humara admi ghar me hai.
Koi bi nah ihai, gharke baju vale aagbujaya.
Hamare bhabi Gousia Begum hospital ko laya".

15. According to the evidence of PW.1 (Khaja Bee), an independent witness who has no family ties to either of the appellant or the deceased resides in the same neighbourhood as of the deceased and the Md. 3 appellant.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Her testimony confirms that the appellant has a habit of consuming alcohol, often returning home under its influence and instigating quarrels with his wife.
On the day of the incident the appellant and the deceased entered their home and locked the doors.
Shortly after she heard the screams of the deceased, despite her attempts to gain entry by knocking, the appellant who was inside did not open the door.

The local residents broke the door open and they found the deceased engulfed in flames, quickly doused her with water, wrapped her in a blanket to extinguish the fire and rushed her to Gandhi Hospital in an ambulance.
PW.1 stated that the deceased told her that it was the appellant who had doused her in kerosene and set her ablaze.
16. Similarly is the evidence of PW.2 (Gousia Begum) and PW.3 (Miraj) who arrived at the scene of occurrence and found the deceased already suffering from burn injuries and seated in the front yard.

Upon questioning the deceased, PW.2 was informed that the appellant had doused her with kerosene and ignited the fire with a match stick and the appellant was reportedly present beside the deceased at that time.

The testimonies of P.Ws1 to 3 confirm the presence of the appellant in the house during the incident which show that the appellant made no effort to extinguish the fire or to save his wife, for reasons only known to him.
The defence did not question PWs.1 to 3 on this matter.

Likewise, the evidence of PW4 to 8 has corroborated the evidence of the PWs.1 to 3.
17.

According to PW.11 who recorded the statement of the deceased under Ex.A4 and read the contents to her and then obtained her thumb impression Ex.P4 indicates that the appellant poured kerosene on the deceased and that she set herself on fire.

18. According to the evidence of P.W12, the Magistrate, where he recorded dying declaration of the deceased in which she stated that her husband set her on fire due to doubts about her chastity held the declaration to be true, voluntary, and free from external influence.

The statement is consistent and unchallenged, corroborated by witnesses, and the police statements under Section 161 of Cr.P.C.
implicate the appellant.
The appellant's failure to assist the victim during the incident indicates his guilt.
There is no evidence suggesting the victim was tutored or that the statement was fabricated.
Thus, the dying declaration is credible and reliable.

Therefore, the Trail Court having appreciated all these facts and while analysing and examining the evidence of the material evidence, came to the correct conclusion and rightly found the appellant herein guilty for the offence under Section 302 of IPC.
19.

The evidence of PWs.1 to 6 prove that the deceased suffered with burn injuries and the evidence of PW.11 and PW.12 prove that the deceased made statements before these two witnesses attributing to the offence for the murder.

PW.14, the Doctor, who conducted post- mortem examination over the dead body of the deceased testified the cause of death was due to burns suffered on 26.04.2012.
20.

In adjudicating the present case, it is pertinent to underscore that the dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate carries a higher evidentiary value compared to an earlier declaration made to the police.
The declarations recorded by a Magistrate are generally more reliable due to the formal safeguards ensuring voluntariness and absence of coercion.
Such declarations are given precedence, especially when inconsistencies arise between multiple statements.

This Court emphasized that each dying declaration must be scrutinized independently, and in the presence of Md. Rafeeq, Hyd., vs State Of Telangana, Rep. Pp., on 11 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/154949575/
4 conflicting statements, the one recorded by a Magistrate is to be preferred, provided it is truthful and free from suspicion.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This approach ensures the administration of justice is both fair and thorough, giving due weight to the declarations made in circumstances carrying the utmost gravity.

21. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Abhishek Sharma vs. State (Govt. of NCT Delhi) 1 in paragraph Nos.8 and 9 held as under:
"8. Before proceeding to the merits of this matter, it would be appropriate to appreciate the various principles of law laid down by this court in regard to cases involving multiple dying declarations.
1 2023 SCC OnLine SC 1358 8.1 This Court in Kamla v. State of Punjab 2 has held:
"5.

entities.text: Abhishek Sharma vs. State (Govt. of NCT Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is well settled that dying declaration can form the sole basis of conviction provided that it is free from infirmities and satisfies various tests (vide Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay [AIR 1958 SC 22 : 1958 SCR 552 : 1958 Cri LJ 106] ).

entities.text: vide Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay [AIR 1958 SC 22 : 1958 SCR 552 : 1958 Cri LJ 106]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The ratio laid down in this case has been referred to in a number of subsequent cases with approval.

It is also settled in all those cases that the statement should be consistent throughout if the deceased had several opportunities of making such dying declarations, that is to say, if there are more than one dying declaration, they should be consistent.
If a dying declaration is found to be voluntary, reliable and made in fit mental condition, it can be relied upon without even any corroboration.

In a case where there are more than one dying declaration if some inconsistencies are noticed between one and the other, the court has to examine the nature of the inconsistencies namely whether they are material or not.
In scrutinising the contents of various dying declarations, in such a situation, the court has to examine the same in the light of the various surrounding facts and circumstances."

8.2 In State of Punjav v. Parveen Kumar 3, this court further observed:
"10. ....

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The court must be satisfied that the dying declaration is truthful.
If there are two dying declarations giving two different versions, a serious doubt is created about the truthfulness of the dying declarations.
It may be that if there was any other reliable evidence on record, this court could have considered such corroborative evidence to test the truthfulness of the dying declarations..."
8.3 In Amol Singh v. State of M.P.4, 2 (1993) 1 SCC 1(2-Judge Bench) 3 (2005) 9 SCC 769 (2-Judge Bench) 4 (2008) 5 SCC 468 ( 2-Judge Bench) "13.

While scrutinising the contents of various dying declarations, in such a situation, the court has to examine the same in the light of the various surrounding facts and circumstances."

sentences.text: In case there are multiple dying declarations and there are inconsistencies between them, generally, the dying declaration recorded by the higher officer like a Magistrate can be relied upon, provided that there is no circumstance giving rise to any suspicion about its truthfulness.

In case there are circumstances wherein the declaration had been made, not voluntarily and even otherwise, it is not supported by the other evidence, the court has to scrutinise the facts of an individual case very carefully and take a decision as to which of the declarations is worth reliance."
This judgment was also referred to by this court recently in Makhan Singh v. State of Haryana 6 8.5

" 15. When there are multiple dying declarations, each dying declaration has to be separately assessed and evaluated and assessed independently on its own merit as to its evidentiary value and one cannot be rejected because of certain variations in the other."

A survey of the decisions would show that the principles of declarations can be culled out as follows:
....
31.6.
However, there may be cases where there are more than one dying declaration.
If there are more than one dying declaration, the dying declarations may entirely agree with one another.
There may be dying declarations where inconsistencies between the declarations emerge.
The extent of the inconsistencies would then have to be considered by the court.
The inconsistencies may turn out to be reconcilable.

31.7. In such cases, where the inconsistencies go to some matter of detail or description but is incriminatory in nature as far as the Accused is concerned, the court would look to the material on record to conclude as to which dying declaration is to be relied on unless it be shown that they are unreliable;
31.8.

The third category of cases is that where there are more than one dying declaration and inconsistencies between the declarations are absolute and the dying declarations are irreconcilable being repugnant to one another.
In a dying declaration, the Accused may not be blamed at all and the cause of death may be placed at the doorstep of an unfortunate accident.
This may be followed up by another dying declaration which is diametrically opposed to the first dying declaration.

In Md. Rafeeq, Hyd., vs State Of Telangana, Rep. Pp., on 11 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/154949575/
6 fact, in that scenario, it may not be a question of an inconsistent dying declaration buta dying declaration which is completely opposed to the dying declaration which is given earlier.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There may be more than two."

8.7 In Uttam v. State of Maharashtra 9, this court observed:
"15.

In cases involving multiple dying declarations made by the deceased, the question that arises for consideration is as to which of the 9 (2022) 8 SCC 576 (2-Judge Bench) said dying declarations ought to be believed by the court and what would be the guiding factors for arriving at a just and lawful conclusion.
The problem becomes all the more knotty when the dying declarations made by the deceased are found to be contradictory.

Faced with such a situation, the court would be expected to carefully scrutinise the evidence to find out as to which of the dying declarations can be corroborated by other material evidence produced by the prosecution.

Of equal significance is the condition of the deceased at the relevant point in time, the medical evidence brought on record that would indicate the physical and mental fitness of the deceased, the scope of the close relatives/family members having influenced/tutored the deceased and all the other attendant circumstances that would help the court in exercise of its discretion."

In other words, inconsistencies between such statements should be 'material' for its credibility to be shaken;
9.3
When inconsistencies are found between various dying declarations, other evidence available on record may be considered for the purposes of corroboration of the contents of dying declarations.
9.4 The statement treated as a dying declaration must be interpreted in light of surrounding facts and circumstances.
9.5 Each declaration must be scrutinized on its own merits.
The court has to examine upon which of the statements reliance can be placed in order for the case to proceed further.

9.6 When there are inconsistencies, the statement that has been recorded by a Magistrate or like higher officer can be relied on, subject to the indispensable qualities of truthfulness and being free of suspicion.

22.

For all the aforesaid reasons and the judicial precedents referred above, we are of the considered opinion that the evidences adduced by the prosecution witnesses as also upon scrutiny of the dying declaration, all of which have been discussed in preceding paragraphs, this Bench finds that the prosecution has been able to prove its case against the appellant beyond all the reasonable doubts.
Thus, affirming the judgment of conviction passed by the Trial Court, the instant appeal stands dismissed.
No costs.
23. As a sequel, miscellaneous applications pending if any, shall stand closed.

9. Having considered various pronouncements of this court, the following principles emerge, for a Court to consider when dealing with a case involving multiple dying declarations:
9.1 The primary requirement for all dying declarations is that they should be voluntary and reliable and that such statements should be in a fit state of mind;
9.2 All dying declarations should be consistent.
In other words, inconsistencies between such statements should be 'material' for its credibility to be shaken;
9.3
When inconsistencies are found between various dying declarations, other evidence available on record may be considered for the purposes of corroboration of the contents of dying declarations.
9.6 When there are inconsistencies, the statement that has been recorded by a Magistrate or like higher officer can be relied on, subject to the indispensable qualities of truthfulness and being free of suspicion.
